units.spoken: REINFORCE and the Baseline
Learn from whole games, then subtract the usual result so each lesson is less noisy.
How can a Pong paddle learn which moves to make from nothing but the points it wins and loses?
The agent picks the moves. A state is its situation right now, a move, or action, is one choice it can make, and a reward is the number the world hands back after each move.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state.
The return is all the reward still to come, later rewards counted a little less; the discount gamma sets how much less.
A state's value V of s is the return the agent expects from state s. A move's value Q of s and a is the return it expects after making move a in state s.

sections.section: 1 A Pong paddle that learns from points

units.spoken: Section one, A Pong paddle that learns from points

In Atari Pong each player moves a paddle up and down to hit the ball back past the other. The state is the screen, a stack of the last few frames so the ball's direction shows. The moves are up, stay and down, one every few frames; one such move is one step. The reward is plus 1 for a point won, minus 1 for a point lost and 0 on every other step. One episode is one full game. J, the average points per game, counts later points a little less: the number learning tries to raise.

Take a look at this figure. The whole game is a screen: the paddle sees the ball coming and has three moves, up, stay, or down. The state is that screen, and the reward is a point won or lost. Everything the paddle learns comes from those points.

Figure 1 shows the running example: Atari Pong, the agent's paddle on the right and the other player on the left, with the ball traveling between them. Take the agent's paddle: it sits on the right, orange, and its job is to hit the ball back past the other player.

sections.section: 2 A network that outputs move chances

units.spoken: Section two, A network that outputs move chances
Value methods such as Q-Learning and Deep Q-Networks (DQN) learn how good every move is, then play the best one. The network learns the choice itself: one chance per move on each screen.

What this figure is teaching is that the network learns the choice itself. The screen goes in and one chance per move comes out, so the paddle draws its move from those chances instead of picking the best-scored one.
Figure 2 shows the chances coming out largest for up on the screen shown, and up is the move drawn.

The network that does this is the policy network. For Pong it gives three raw outputs, one per move, and a softmax turns them into three chances that add to one. Its weights are written theta, and the chance it gives move a on screen s is pi sub theta of a given s.

sections.section: 3 Make the moves before a point was won more likely

units.spoken: Section three, Make the moves before a point was won more likely
Push each move by its credit

Picture a Pong rally: the paddle slides up, holds still, slides down, and halfway through it wins a point. The moves just before that point set it up, so they deserve the credit and the moves before a lost point deserve the blame.

How. A method that learns this way is a policy-gradient method: each move is pushed by its credit, a number saying how well things turned out after it, with positive credit raising the move's chance and negative credit lowering it.
When it works, the paddle repeats the moves that won points and drops the ones that lost them, so its play sharpens game by game.

Take a look at this figure. A point at the end of a rally reaches back to the moves before it: the moves that set up the won point get more likely, and the moves before the lost point get less likely. The credit is the points that followed each move.

Figure 3 runs the timeline left to right, each mark one move, with a green check where a point is won and a red cross where one is lost; green up arrows stand under the moves before the won point and red down arrows under the moves before the lost point.
Pushing a move up means a small change to theta that raises that move's chance on that screen; the other two drop, since the three add to one.
Policy-gradient methods differ in the credit they use; here the credit is the points that followed each move.

sections.section: 4 Weighting each move by the points that followed

units.spoken: Section four, Weighting each move by the points that followed
One game, one push per move
Picture the whole game as a finished story: every move in it already happened, and the points after each move are already known.

How. REINFORCE plays one full game, works out each move’s return, and pushes each move by its own return. Learning from finished games, rather than from a guess of what comes next, is called Monte Carlo learning.
When it works, a single finished game is enough to teach the paddle, because every move in it already has the points that followed it.

To turn this into a loss to minimize, reuse the classification loss of supervised learning, cross-entropy, which scores each move by the log of its chance, with the move actually played as the label, scaled by the return that followed it. The return stays fixed during the update: it is a number from the game just played, and the weights cannot change it.

Why the log? A move played often gets pushed often, just because it is common. The log undoes that. The slope of a log chance is the slope of the chance itself, divided by that chance. So the more common a move is, the smaller each of its pushes.

Equation 1. REINFORCE learns from whole games, so it needs one number that scores each step by the points that followed it. A chess player judging a move by the game that followed it faces the same need.
Take a look at this equation. It scores each move by the points that followed it.

The return line. G sub t is the return from step t on. The sum over k adds the rewards after step t. It runs to T minus one, the last step. Gamma to the k minus t shrinks each later reward. R sub k plus one is the reward after step k. At k equals t the next reward counts whole, and each later reward is shrunk by gamma. The return is r sub t plus one, plus gamma times r sub t plus two, plus gamma squared times r sub t plus three. Intuitively, the return is the points that followed, with later points counted less.
termList: gamma to the k minus t

units.spoken: Intuition. A move can only claim the points that come after it, so this line adds those points into one number to push by.

Example. Take a game where the paddle wins a point halfway through and loses one near the end: the moves before the won point count it almost whole, while the first moves count it shrunk by the steps between.

The loss line. L sub G of theta is the REINFORCE loss. Pi sub theta gives the chance of move a sub t on screen s sub t. The log of that chance is what the loss weighs. G sub t is the return that followed the move. The minus makes the sum a loss to minimize. The sum over t adds over every step. G sub t is held fixed: the loss treats it as a number, not a function of theta. A move with a high return is pushed up, and one with a low return is pushed down. Intuitively, each move is pushed by the points that followed it.
termList: pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. One number must turn a finished game into a push on every move in it. This line is that number.
Example. Take the moves before the won point: the loss pushes them up, and the moves before the lost point down.
So the whole card says this: the return scores each move by the points that followed it, and the loss pushes each move’s chance by that score.

sections.section: 5 Why one game is a noisy judge

units.spoken: Section five, Why one game is a noisy judge
The bad move that still gets pushed up
Picture the paddle winning a point after a bad down move that let the ball slip past. The points after that move are high anyway, so the bad move gets pushed up just like the good ones.
How. The true push is an average over every game the paddle could play, but REINFORCE estimates it from the one game it just played, so each update carries that game's luck.
When it works, the paddle still learns over many games, because the lucky pushes and the unlucky ones average out, even though any single update can point the wrong way.

Here is the point of this figure. The paddle makes a bad move, down while the ball comes in high, and still wins the points after it. Every move before that point gets pushed up, including the bad one, because one game cannot tell which move earned the point.

Figure 4 shows why one game is a noisy judge: the points after a move are all the evidence one game gives about it, so the update has no way to tell a move that earned the point from one that only came before it.
Section six, Subtracting the usual result
The advantage from one game

Picture two screens: on one the paddle is well placed and points usually follow, on the other it is badly placed and points rarely follow. What matters is whether a move did better or worse than usual from that screen.

How. A baseline is that usual result, subtracted from the return. The return minus the guess is the move's advantage, how much better than usual it did. A second network, the value network, learns the guess.
When it works, the pushes carry less noise, because a move is pushed up only when it beats the usual result and down when it falls short, instead of by the raw points that followed it.
The value network looks at the screen and outputs one number, V sub phi of s, its guess of the usual result. Phi stands for its weights, as theta does for the policy network.
The advantage from one game is only an estimate, so it wears a hat, the mark for an estimate: A hat sub t.
Equation 2. One game is a noisy judge of a move, so each move is judged against what its screen usually returns. A coach who scores a player against the team's usual result faces the same need.
Take a look at this equation. It scores each move against the usual result.

The advantage line. A hat sub t is the advantage of the move at step t. G sub t is the return from step t on. V sub phi of s sub t is the value network’s guess for the screen. The hat means estimate: one game is one sample of all the games the paddle could have played. Minus the guess takes off the usual result. A move that beats the guess has a positive advantage, and one that falls short has a negative one. Intuitively, a move counts only when it beats what its screen usually returns.
termList: V sub phi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. This line takes the return and subtracts the usual result, so only the edge over usual counts.

Example. Take a screen where the ball is already past the paddle, so the next point is almost always lost: the value network’s guess there is low, so every move there is pushed down unless it beats the guess.

The baseline loss line. L sub A hat of theta is the baseline loss. Pi sub theta gives the chance of move a sub t on screen s sub t. The log of that chance is what the loss weighs. A hat sub t is the advantage, the return minus the value network’s guess. The minus turns the weighted sum into a loss to minimize. A hat sub t is held fixed, as the return was in the REINFORCE loss. Intuitively, each move is pushed by its edge over usual, not by the raw points.
termList: L sub A hat of theta
pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. The advantage must reach every move in the game. This line swaps it in for the return in the REINFORCE loss.
Example. Take the circled bad move of Figure 4: its return is high, yet the usual result from its screen is higher still, so its advantage is negative and the loss pushes it down.

The value loss line. L sub V of phi is the value loss. G sub t minus V sub phi of s sub t is the gap between the return and the guess. Squaring the gap makes a miss in either direction count. Only phi changes through this line. Making it smaller pulls the guess toward the real return. Intuitively, a good guess makes the advantage honest.
termList: G sub t minus V sub phi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. The advantage is only as good as the guess it subtracts. This line teaches the value network to guess better.
Example. Take the screens late in a lost game: the returns there are low, so the value loss pulls the guess for those screens down toward them.
A push is biased when, averaged over many games, it points somewhere other than the direction that raises J, the average points per game.

The baseline must depend only on the screen, never on the move made there. Then subtracting it adds no bias. The baseline's part of a single move's push is the slope of its log chance, times the baseline. Averaged over the moves, each push is weighted by that move's chance: the chance-weighted pushes added together give the baseline times the slope of all the chances added together. The chances always add to one, so their slope is zero, and on average the baseline's pushes cancel.
Section seven, Keeping the paddle undecided
The price of certainty
Picture the paddle winning a few points by staying still: every push raises stay a little more, until up and down are almost never tried and the paddle never finds out that moving up wins more.

How. Entropy is how undecided the policy is, and the entropy bonus rewards the policy for staying undecided, so it keeps trying moves it rarely picks. The entropy weight c sub H sets how much the loss pays for staying undecided.
When it works, the paddle still tries the moves it rarely picks, so it can still find the better move.

Take a look at this figure. Without the bonus, stay takes almost all the chance and the paddle stops trying the other moves. With the bonus, up and down keep a sliver, so the paddle stays undecided and can still find the better move.
Figure 5 puts the two cases side by side: on the left the stay bar takes almost all the chance, so the paddle is decided; on the right stay is still largest, so the paddle stays undecided.
Equation 3. A paddle that wins a few points by staying still stops trying the other moves, so the loss pays it to stay undecided. A player who only ever tries one opening faces the same trap.
Take a look at this equation. It pays the paddle to stay undecided.

The entropy line. H is the entropy, how undecided the policy is. Pi sub theta of dot given s is the policy on screen s. The dot stands for all three chances. Pi sub theta of a given s is the chance of move a. The log of that chance is what each term weighs. The sum over a adds over the moves. The minus in front makes H positive, since a log below one is negative. When the moves are about equally likely H is high; when one move is certain H is zero. Intuitively, entropy measures how undecided the chances still are.
termList: pi sub theta of a given s

units.spoken: Intuition. A paddle that locks onto one move stops learning. This line measures how undecided its chances still are.
Example. Take the three moves sharing chance equally: each term is the same and the entropy is at its highest.

The total loss line. L sub total is the total loss. L sub A hat of theta is the baseline loss, pushing toward good moves. L sub V of phi is the value loss, fitting the value network. c sub H is the entropy weight. H of pi sub theta is the entropy on screen s sub t. Minus the entropy term takes off the bonus. The minus means training pays a small price for certainty. Raising c sub H keeps the paddle undecided longer, while lowering it lets it commit sooner. The value loss changes only phi; the rest changes only theta. Intuitively, one update minimizes all three at once.
termList: L sub A hat of theta

units.spoken: Intuition. The loss must pay the policy to stay undecided. This line takes a small entropy bonus off the total.
Example. Take a screen where stay has won lately, so it gets most of the chance: the entropy there is near zero, so the bonus keeps a sliver on up and down for the paddle to try.
Together, the two lines say one thing: measure how undecided the policy is, then pay it a small bonus to stay that way.
Section eight, Step through one REINFORCE update
Put together, one update has four ideas: the return, the advantage, the value fit and the entropy bonus.

What this figure is teaching is that one update is one rally turned into pushes. The game gives every move a return, the advantage scores each move against the usual result, the value network is fitted to the returns, and the bonus keeps the paddle undecided. The seven stages light the six lines in order, from the return to the total.

Try stepping through the seven stages with the Next button. Watch which line lights at each stage: only the line that stage uses. The return is built first, then each move is pushed by its score, then scored against the usual result, and the bonus holds the paddle undecided at the end.
One Pong rally shows how a whole game becomes one push on every move it contained. This walkthrough follows one Pong update through Equations 1, 2 and 3.
Take a look at this equation. One rally becomes one push on every move it contained.

The return line. G sub t is the return of step t. The sum over k adds the rewards after step t, up to T minus one, the last step. Gamma to the k minus t shrinks each later reward. R sub k plus one is the reward after step k. A point counts most for the move just before it and less for earlier moves. A lost point at the end pulls every earlier score down. Intuitively, every move gets one number to push by, the points that followed it.
termList: gamma to the k minus t

units.spoken: Intuition. Stage 1 of the walkthrough: this line gives every move one number to push by, the points that followed it, with later points counted less.
Example. Take step 4, just before the first won point: the point that follows counts whole, so its return is the biggest of the game.

The loss line. L sub G of theta is the REINFORCE loss. Pi sub theta gives the chance of move a sub t on screen s sub t. The log of that chance is what the loss weighs. G sub t is the return that followed the move. Minimizing this loss raises the log chance of moves with a positive return and lowers it where the return is negative. Intuitively, the push on each move follows its own score.
termList: pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Stage 2: this line weighs each move’s log chance by its score, so the push on a move follows the points after it.
Example. Take the circled bad move: its return is high, so this line counts it as a move worth repeating, even though the move itself was bad.

The advantage line. A hat sub t is the advantage of the move at step t. G sub t is the return from step t on. V sub phi of s sub t is the value network’s guess for the screen. The sign of the advantage is what matters here: a move that beats its screen’s usual result counts as good even when its return is small, and a move that falls short counts as bad even when its return is high. Intuitively, a move counts only when it beats what its screen usually returns.
termList: V sub phi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Stage 3: this line scores each move against the usual result, so a move counts only when it beats what its screen usually returns.
Example. Take the circled bad move: the line judges it against its own screen, not against the game’s points, so it counts as a bad move.

The baseline loss line. L sub A hat of theta is the baseline loss. Pi sub theta gives the chance of move a sub t on screen s sub t. The log of that chance is what the loss weighs. A hat sub t is the advantage, the return minus the value network’s guess. The advantage replaces the return as the weight, so a move is pushed up only when it beat its screen’s usual result, and pushed down when it fell short. Intuitively, one update shifts the policy toward the moves that beat the usual result.
termList: L sub A hat of theta
pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Stages 4 and 5: this line is the REINFORCE loss with the advantage in place of the return.
Example. Take the circled screen: down fell short of the usual result there, so this line takes chance away from down and gives it to up and stay.

The value loss line. L sub V of phi is the value loss. G sub t minus V sub phi of s sub t is the gap between the return and the guess. Squaring the gap makes a miss in either direction count. Minimizing it pulls the guess toward the real return on every screen in the game. Intuitively, the value network learns to guess better.
termList: G sub t minus V sub phi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Stage 6: this line teaches the value network, pulling its guess toward the returns the game actually gave.
Example. Take the tallest bar, at step 4: the guess there was far below the real return, so this line pulls it up the most.

The total loss line. L sub total is the total loss. L sub A hat of theta is the baseline loss, pushing toward good moves. L sub V of phi is the value loss, fitting the value network. c sub H is the entropy weight. H of pi sub theta is the entropy on screen s sub t. Minus the entropy term takes off the bonus. The entropy term is the only part that rewards indecision: without it the total would let the policy commit to one move. Intuitively, add up the points, score each move, fit the value, and pay a small price for certainty, all in one loss.
termList: L sub A hat of theta

units.spoken: Intuition. Stage 7: this line puts the bonus into the total, so the update keeps the paddle undecided.
Example. Take the gauge: the white mark is where the paddle would end on the pushes alone, and the bonus holds it further from certain.

Figure 6 shows one game and one update: the game, the points that followed each step, the push on each move, and the chances on the circled screen. Stages 1 to 7 light the six lines in order, from the return to the total. The gauge at the bottom shows how undecided the paddle is.

sections.section: 9 The update written out as code

units.spoken: Section nine, The update written out as code

Picture the whole update as one short script: play a game, work out each move’s return, and push. A toy REINFORCE for Pong, to read rather than run. Pong has six actions: stay, fire, up, down, up plus fire and down plus fire, and we keep up, stay and down because fire does nothing useful here. Gymnasium is the library that runs the game, and ale py, the Atari plugin, plugs the Atari games into it. The game is made with frameskip 1, so it skips no frames of its own, and the preprocessing repeats each move over four frames, so one move is one step. The wrappers prepare the screen: one turns each frame gray and smaller, one stacks four frames so the ball’s direction shows, and Categorical, the move picker, draws a move from the policy’s chances. Each screen is divided by 255, so its pixels run from 0 to 1, and unsqueeze zero adds a batch of one, so the network sees one screen at a time. Sampling runs under no grad, so choosing the move builds no gradients. The move list holds Pong’s own codes for up, stay and down.
This code runs one REINFORCE update on a whole game.
1. The return of every step, added up backward from the last reward.
2. The policy network’s logits, its raw outputs before the softmax; logp is the log chance of each move taken, as in the REINFORCE loss.
3. The value loss: the value network’s guess for every screen and its squared gap to the return.
4. The advantage and the baseline loss: adv is A hat sub t, held fixed by detach, and pg loss is L sub A hat.

5. The total loss, with the entropy of the move distribution as its entropy line; zero grad clears the last update’s gradients, the backward call works out every gradient and the optimizer update is one Adam update.

6. The settings, named in the code. DISCOUNT 0.99 is the discount, FRAMES 4 is the number of stacked frames, N MOVES 3 is the number of moves, and N EPISODES 10 is the number of toy episodes. C ENTROPY 0.01 is the entropy weight and LEARNING RATE 0.0001 is the learning rate. The first layer scans the stacked frames for patterns, and C1 32 counts how many patterns it looks for. The second layer does the same on the result, and C2 64 counts its patterns. Flattening stacks those into one long list, and FLAT 5184 counts the numbers in it. The next layer turns that list into a list of HIDDEN 512 numbers, and the last layer turns those numbers into the move scores. The network turns the stacked frames into move chances.

sections.section: 10 How a baseline narrows the spread

units.spoken: Section ten, How a baseline narrows the spread
The learning rate eta, the lr in the code, sets how big a step each update takes.

A less noisy push makes separate training runs end closer together. How far apart they end is the spread. A baseline set above the usual result makes most pushes point the wrong way, so the training runs spread out again.

The tool sets its own win chances, for illustration: up is the most likely winner, then stay, then down. Its baseline is the exact usual result, worked out from those win chances, not a value a network learned.

Here is the point of this figure. Thirty training runs of the same forty games end far apart without a baseline, because each run carries its own luck. With the usual-result baseline the runs end close together, so the spread shrinks. The bars below are each game's push on the chance of up.

Try the three baselines and the two step sizes. With the usual-result baseline, watch the training runs end close together. Switch to no baseline with a large step and watch them spread apart instead. A baseline set too high pushes most moves the wrong way, so the runs spread out again.

Figure 7 shows thirty training runs of forty games: the chance of up, the best move here, over the games, with the end strip showing where each training run ends. The thick line is one training run, the faint lines the other twenty-nine, and the shaded band is how far apart the training runs end, against the dashed band for the usual-result baseline.

sections.section: 11 How to set up each update

units.spoken: Section eleven, How to set up each update

This table gathers the settings for REINFORCE with a baseline. The learning rate is ten to the minus four: bigger steps can collapse the chances onto one move, while smaller steps learn steadier but slower. The discount is 0.99: a higher discount counts far-off points more, which cuts bias but adds noise, while a lower one counts only near points, which cuts noise but adds bias. The entropy weight is 0.01: a higher weight keeps the paddle undecided longer so it tries more but settles slower, while a lower one lets it commit sooner but risks locking onto one move.

Table 1 gathers the settings for REINFORCE with a baseline: the learning rate, the discount and the entropy weight, each with its value and what raising or lowering it does. Each row names its source, from the Pong post to the PyTorch cart-pole example, so the values are the ones the field uses, not guesses.

Each update runs once per finished game, and what carries over between updates is the two networks’ weights and the optimizer’s running averages. One update’s time grows with the length of the game it just played, and its memory is the game itself: the states, moves and rewards it must keep until the update runs.
Normalize the returns: shift and scale them so each update’s returns average zero and have a standard deviation of one.
Average several games into one update, so the update then runs once per batch of games instead of once per finished game.
Section twelve, When REINFORCE fits
REINFORCE fits short games. A long game piles up many moves before the point, so each push carries the whole game's luck.
Section thirteen, What breaks REINFORCE
Five symptoms, five fixes
Picture a paddle after a long night of training that still loses: its training runs end far apart, its chances have collapsed onto one move, and it never settles on anything better.
How. Each break has its own cause: no baseline, a baseline that sees the move, a step too big, an entropy weight set too low or too high, and games too long to tell which move deserves the credit.

When it works, read the symptom and name the fix: subtract a learned value, let the baseline see only the screen, lower the step, raise or lower the entropy weight to fit the symptom, or judge moves sooner.

This table gathers what breaks REINFORCE: five symptoms, each with its cause and its fix. Training runs that end far apart and learn slowly come from having no baseline, and the fix is to subtract a learned value. A paddle that drifts toward worse moves has a baseline that depends on the move, so the push is biased, and the fix is to let the baseline see only the screen. Chances that collapse onto one move come from a learning rate too high or an entropy weight too small, and the fix is to lower eta or raise c sub H. A paddle that never commits has an entropy weight too large, and the fix is to lower c sub H. Learning that barely moves in very long games comes from each move’s share of the result being hard to tell apart, and the fix is to judge moves sooner.
Table 2 gathers what breaks REINFORCE: five symptoms, each with its cause and its fix.

sections.section: 14 Judging each move before the game ends

units.spoken: Section fourteen, Judging each move before the game ends
What if the value network’s guess stood in for the points still to come, so each move could be judged a few steps later instead of at the end of the game?
Judging each move before the game ends is the idea behind Actor-Critic, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) builds on that.
Aligning Language Models with RL applies the same push to the text a language model writes.
